newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia bonds eye Fed move but focus on local troubles.
newsitem.headline: Asia bonds eye Fed move but focus on local troubles.

text.p: The U.S. Federal Reserve's move to raise short-term rates a slim quarter point is expected to have a modest impact on Asian debt markets, with problems closer to home seen looming larger, bankers said on Wednesday.

"Investors will be a bit more cautious about what they buy, but fundamentally I don't see a sea change for Asian borrowers," said Allen Cutler, head of Asian debt capital markets at Lehman Brothers in Hong Kong.
The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC), the Fed's policymaking arm, on Tuesday raised the key federal funds rate to 5.5 percent in a move that was widely expected.
The FOMC left the discount rate unchanged at 5.0 percent.
Because the action was so well anticipated, the reaction in the U.S. bond markets was muted, Asian analysts said.
It was a similar story in the Asian debt markets, they said.
Emerging market bonds, including Asian credits, took a hit in late February after Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan told Congress it was important to act pre-emptively on inflation.
With much of the damage already done, traders in Asia said reaction to the actual rate hike was modest.
"I don't think we will see spreads tightening, but I don't think we will see them widening either," said Lehman's Cutler.
But he acknowledged that the market has changed from earlier this year, when investors snapped up Asian issues.

"We have moved from what we had at the beginning of the year -- a sellers' market where investors would take anything they could get their hands on -- to a something with a bit more equilibrium," he said.
With Asia growing by leaps and bounds and local debt markets still underdeveloped, bankers said Asian firms wishing to expand would continue to tap international markets for funding.
But Asian issuers and investors, like their counterparts elsewhere, will be closely monitoring U.S. economic data to assess the likelihood of further rate hikes.
More aggressive tightening would have a bigger impact on the markets, bankers said.
In the meantime, problems closer to home are occupying the minds of Asian debt market professionals, bankers said.

"One of the reasons why there was such a muted reaction to the Fed move was that there are a lot of other market moving factors that are eclipsing this," said Rey Espinelli, vice president of new issues at BA Asia.
Korean banks, a mainstay of the Asian debt markets, have virtually disappeared from the scene after the default of Hanbo Steel jolted the country's financial markets.
The more recent failure of Sammi Steel Co and speculation that more Korean companies may be in trouble have depressed demand for Korean bank and corporate credits.
Thai borrowers also have turned quiet as the government grapples with Thailand's troubled banking sector.
Bankers also noted that many Asian borrowers, particularly the banks, usually issue floating rather than fixed rate paper.
As a result, the Fed's action has a minimal effect on their borrowing costs as long as Asian countries -- many of which have currencies that follow the the U.S. dollar -- avoid rate hikes.
If local banks were to face higher funding costs, the companies that borrow from them through loans and loan-style floating notes eventually could feel the pain, bankers said.
Hong Kong already has taken the plunge.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority raised its own discount rate, the Liquidity Adjustment Rate, by 25 basis points on Wednesday. Local banks followed with increases in prime rates of the same margin.
